title: A Museum Trip and Password Safety

listening1.context: You are going to hear a conversation between Muna and Sultan.

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: Hello, Sultan! Our teacher says that the class trip to the museum is next week. Have you chosen the day?

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: Not yet. Mrs Zahra said we can go on Monday or Wednesday. I prefer Monday, but there is a football match on that day.

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: Then Wednesday is better. The museum has a special show about ancient Egypt, and I really want to see it.

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: Me too. Do you know how we'll travel? The school bus is too small for the whole class.

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: I heard that we'll go by two buses, and they will leave at eight o'clock. Don't be late!

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: I won't. My mother will drive me to school at seven thirty. What is the first thing we'll see there?

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: The guide said we'll start with the mummies. They are about three thousand years old, and people wrapped them with cloth.

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: Amazing! And after that? I'd like to see the famous golden mask.

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: That's in the second hall. The guide told me it belongs to a young king called Tutankhamun, who died when he was about eighteen.

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: Poor boy! Are we allowed to take photographs inside?

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: Yes, but we can't use a flash, because it damages the old objects. We also can't touch anything.

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: I understand. Do we need to bring any money?

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: Only a little. The ticket is free for school groups, but lunch isn't. We'll eat in the museum cafe, and a sandwich costs one rial.

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: That's cheap. And what should we do after lunch?

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: There is a workshop where students can make a small clay vase like the Egyptians did. I'm looking forward to it.

script.speaker: Sultan
script.text: It sounds like fun. Don't forget that we must write a short report about the trip. Mrs Zahra wants it by Sunday.

script.speaker: Muna
script.text: Oh yes, I almost forgot. Thanks for reminding me!

items.q: Which day will the class go to the museum?
What time will the buses leave?
What will the students see first?
How old was Tutankhamun when he died?
What can students NOT use inside the museum?
How much is a sandwich in the museum cafe?
When must the students give the report to the teacher?

listening2.context: You are going to hear a talk about password safety.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Hello, everybody. Today I am going to talk about how to keep your passwords safe online.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: We use passwords every day. We need them for our e-mail, our games, our social media and our school accounts. A password is like a key. If a stranger finds your key, he can enter your home. In the same way, a stranger who finds your password can enter your account.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So, what makes a strong password? First, it must be long. Experts say that a password should have at least twelve letters, numbers and symbols. Short passwords are easy for a computer to guess in a few seconds. Second, it should be difficult to guess. Never use your name, your birthday or the word password. These are the first things that criminals try.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: A good idea is to choose a sentence you can remember, for example, I love eating fresh dates in summer. Then use the first letter of each word and add a few numbers and symbols. The result looks strange to other people, but it is easy for you to remember.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Next, use a different password for every account. Many people use the same password everywhere. If a criminal discovers it once, he can open all of their accounts. Some people use a password manager, a program that keeps all passwords safe, so they need to remember only one.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You should also change your passwords if you think someone knows them. Do not tell your friends your passwords, and do not write them on paper near your computer.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Finally, use two-step login when it is possible. After you write your password, the website sends a code to your phone. Even if somebody learns your password, he cannot enter without the code. This simple step stops most attacks.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Remember, strong passwords protect your photos, your messages and your money. Thank you for listening.

short.q: How many characters should a strong password have at least?
What should you NOT use in a password? Give one example.
What does the website send to your phone for two-step login?

tf.statement: Short passwords are difficult for computers to guess.
You should use a different password for every account.
It is a good idea to write passwords on paper near the computer.
